title: Today in one sentence
text: Stocks fell on Wednesday after the inflation report came in a bit hotter than expected: the S&P 500 fund SPY lost 1.1% and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ lost 2.0%, with chip and space stocks hit hardest; tomorrow, watch TSMC's earnings report.

title: Inflation came in a bit hot
text: Prices in September were 3.7% higher than a year earlier, above the 3.6% economists expected, and up 0.6% from August, as forecast. About half of the monthly rise came from gasoline, which jumped 9.1%. Prices without food and energy rose a calmer 0.3% in the month. When prices rise faster, people worry that interest rates stay high, and that often hurts stocks that are expensive compared with their profits. The Fed meets next on Oct. 27 and 28.

title: Chip and space stocks led the drop
text: Rocket Lab fell 7.8%, Vertiv 6.1%, AMD 5.7%, TSMC 3.4%, Broadcom 3.1% and NVIDIA 3.1%. These companies have big price swings (their beta is high, which means they move more than the market). AMD is the most expensive of the group: its price is about 145 times its yearly profit, so it feels rising rates the most. The Nasdaq stocks in the tech sector fell 1.8% on average.

title: Health and defense went the other way
text: Eli Lilly rose 3.8% and Lockheed Martin 3.6%, and the dividend fund SCHD gained 1.0%, while most of the list fell. In the Nasdaq, healthcare stocks gained 1.3% on average and consumer staples (everyday goods) gained 2.0%. This is why people mix different kinds of companies: when one group falls, another may hold up. One day is not a trend.

title: TSMC reports on Thursday
text: TSMC makes chips for NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom, so its report on Thursday, Oct. 15 is a clue for the whole AI chip world. Earlier this month it said its sales for July to September were a record, about 50% above a year before. The stock closed at $430.00, about 12% below its highest price of the past year ($487.47). The report will also say what TSMC expects for the months ahead.

title: Lesson 7: What is dollar cost averaging?
text: Dollar cost averaging means putting in the same amount of money on a regular schedule, like $100 every month, no matter what the price is. Say a stock costs $10, then $8, then $12. Your $100 buys 10 shares, then 12.5, then 8.33, so you own 30.83 shares for $300. That is about $9.73 each, a little less than the $10 average price, because you automatically buy more when the price is low and fewer when it is high. Today is a good example: SPY fell 1.1%, and a person buying every month would simply get slightly more shares today than yesterday. It does not guarantee a profit and it does not protect from losses, but it takes away the stress of guessing the perfect day.

title: What this covers
text: Prices are from Wednesday's close. Analyst price targets and company numbers are available for NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, GE Aerospace and Lockheed Martin. Broadcom, Vertiv, Rocket Lab, Eli Lilly and Intuitive Surgical have prices and risk scores only. This is information to learn from, not advice to buy or sell anything.
